title: Moving Up (2)

jokes.text: Can't believe Michael Bay spent a billion dollars of his own money to build that for The Rock.
jokes.setup: Andy and Leslie are looking at Alcatraz in San Francisco Bay.
jokes.punchline: Andy genuinely believes the real Alcatraz island was built by Michael Bay as a film set for 'The Rock'.
jokes.explanation: Classic Andy Dwyer stupidity — not random dumbness but specifically movie-brained dumbness. The specificity of 'billion dollars of his own money' elevates it. Strong character integration because only Andy would frame real history through a 90s action movie lens.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Whoa, Alcatraz. Michael Bay built this for The Rock, right?

jokes.text: I can't believe you were able to recite that entire movie, from memory, on the plane ride. You weren't trying to sleep, were you? I couldn't tell, 'cause you had that mask thing over your eyes.
jokes.setup: Andy has just mistaken Alcatraz for a movie set, implying deep familiarity with The Rock.
jokes.punchline: Leslie reveals Andy recited the entire film on the plane while she tried to sleep — and he was so oblivious he didn't notice her sleep mask.
jokes.explanation: Strong callback that deepens the Andy characterization. The addition of the sleep mask detail is a great economy move — it adds a visual gag AND explains why he kept going. The escalation from 'he thinks Alcatraz is a movie set' to 'he recited the whole movie on the flight' lands well.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Were you trying to sleep?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I had my sleep mask on.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What's a sleep mask?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It goes over your eyes so the light doesn't bother you.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Why would you put it over your eyes? Just close your eyes.

jokes.text: 'What happens at a National Parks Conference is compiled and emailed to you in a PDF the following Monday.'
jokes.setup: Leslie says 'you know what they say' about the National Parks Conference, setting up a 'what happens in Vegas' riff.
jokes.punchline: The punchline subverts the expected 'stays here' with the hyper-bureaucratic reality of conference follow-up PDFs — perfectly in character for government workers.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The misdirection is perfectly set up with 'you know what they say,' and the payoff is both a character-specific joke (Leslie Knope lives in a world of bureaucratic follow-up emails) and a sharp observational joke about the mundanity of professional conferences. The specificity of 'PDF the following Monday' is genius economy. Highly quotable and rewatch-worthy because the setup is so clean.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what they say: what happens in a government office stays in a government office. Actually, no, it gets filed in triplicate and sent to the state capital.

jokes.text: That's exactly how they'll be expecting me to try to break in.
jokes.setup: They discuss wanting to see Alcatraz; someone mentions they give tours.
jokes.punchline: Andy rejects the tour option because 'that's exactly how they'll be expecting' him to break in — treating a tourist attraction like an active prison heist.
jokes.explanation: Andy's action-movie brain applied to a completely mundane situation. His earnest belief that he's outsmarting the guards by refusing the tour is delightful character comedy. Good economy — the joke is short and lands clean.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We should take a tour of Alcatraz.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: A tour? Isn't that part of breaking in?

jokes.text: This is the hardest I've worked on anything since... Wow. I've never worked hard on anything. What a cool life!
jokes.setup: Tom is introducing his restaurant opening, speaking with pride about his hard work.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence self-reflection reveals he has literally never worked hard on anything before — and he responds with pure delight rather than shame.
jokes.explanation: Excellent talking-head joke. The mid-sentence pivot where Tom audits his own claim and arrives at the opposite conclusion is structurally beautiful. 'What a cool life!' as a reaction to discovering his own laziness is perfectly Tom — turning a potential character flaw into self-congratulation. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: You know, I've been working really hard on this restaurant, and I gotta say, I'm loving it. The long hours, the stress, the constant problem-solving... it's actually pretty great.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait a minute. Have I ever actually worked hard before? Like, ever?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Oh my God, I haven't. This is amazing. I feel so alive!

jokes.text: They're not even done painting that sign. It says 'Tom's bi.'
jokes.setup: Tom's team is panicking about not being ready for a soft opening.
jokes.punchline: The sign painter has only finished half the word 'Bistro', leaving it reading 'Tom's bi.'
jokes.explanation: Simple visual gag that works through the partially completed sign. The double entendre is a bit of a cheap laugh but executed crisply and in context. Not particularly character-specific but earns its place in the chaos-of-opening sequence.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We have to open tomorrow? I'm wigging out. And not in the fun way where I'm wearing a wig named Kristen.

jokes.text: Actually, no, that's good.
jokes.setup: Someone points out the sign reads 'Tom's bi' as a problem.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately sees this as a marketing asset, not a problem — perfectly in character for a guy who courts any buzz.
jokes.explanation: The callback to the sign joke but the real laugh is Tom's instant pivot to brand opportunity. Strong character integration — Tom's instinct to spin everything into buzz is perfectly captured in two words.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: The sign painter hasn't finished yet. Right now it just says 'Rent.'

jokes.text: 'This little Italian restaurant will put McDonald's out of business' on three. One, two, three! This little Italian restaurant will put McDonald's out of business! ...rise from hell fire!
jokes.setup: Tom leads a rallying cheer about the restaurant beating McDonald's.
jokes.punchline: One employee is on a completely different (demonic) cheer — '...rise from hell fire!' — either mishearing or in a different headspace entirely.
jokes.explanation: Solid absurdist runner. The cheer escalation to satanic imagery is unexpected and funny. Not deeply character-specific but the surprise landing earns a genuine laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, my sign says 'Tom's bi'? That's... actually brilliant for business. People love that kind of thing. Free publicity. I'm keeping it.

jokes.text: Lester Kanopf? Come on, guys, get it together.
jokes.setup: Someone's phone goes off at an inopportune moment.
jokes.punchline: The contact name 'Lester Kanopf' suggests Leslie gave this person a fake/alternate name in their phone — a recurring bit that pays off later.
jokes.explanation: First instance of the 'Lester Kanopf' running gag. On first viewing it's mildly confusing but becomes funnier in retrospect when we see it's Leslie's alias. The deadpan 'Come on, guys' adds to the mystery. Rewatch bonus for sure.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: McDonald's, McDonald's, Kentucky Fried Chicken and a Pizza Hut... BLOOD EVERYWHERE! SATAN IS REAL!

jokes.text: Sorry, Lester. Yours is right here.
jokes.setup: The phone rings with 'Lester Kanopf' displayed.
jokes.punchline: Ben casually calls Leslie 'Lester,' confirming this is her alias — treated completely normally by him.
jokes.explanation: Deepens the Lester Kanopf bit. Ben's total nonchalance about calling his wife by an alias in public is funny. Gets better on rewatch when you understand the full gag.

jokes.text: Liam Bonneville? The Department of the Interior's resident bad boy? Well, now you've got my attention. Let me go grab my autograph book and we'll head out.
jokes.setup: Grant mentions that Liam Bonneville from the Department of the Interior will be at lunch.
jokes.punchline: Leslie treats a government bureaucrat like a rock star, immediately fetching her autograph book.
jokes.explanation: 'The Department of the Interior's resident bad boy' is a great subversion of rockstar language applied to the most niche bureaucratic context. Leslie's autograph book reaction is perfect character comedy — only she would have an autograph book ready for government officials.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: A bad boy! That's what he is!

jokes.text: No idea. (talking head — Ben answering 'What does Gryzzl do?')
jokes.setup: Ben explains they're pitching Pawnee to a tech company called Gryzzl, then someone off-camera asks what Gryzzl does.
jokes.punchline: Cut to Ben's talking head: 'No idea.' Delivered with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: Perfect mockumentary comedic beat. The cut to the talking head 'No idea' is maximum economy — two words, dead-on delivery, lands hard. Ben's competence being undermined by his total ignorance of the company he's pitching to is a great irony. The structure (setup in scene, punchline in confessional) is textbook Parks mockumentary form.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What does Gryzzl actually do?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: You know, I have no idea. I honestly have no idea what Gryzzl does.

jokes.text: Six months ago, I was working in a taco truck. Now, I own one-third of the Portland Trailblazers.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl employee is explaining the company's rapid rise.
jokes.punchline: The escalation from 'taco truck' to 'one-third of an NBA franchise' in six months satirizes Silicon Valley excess and absurd tech wealth.
jokes.explanation: Good satirical shorthand for tech startup absurdity. The specificity of 'one-third of the Portland Trailblazers' (not the Lakers, not a whole team) is a nice detail. Moderate character integration since it's a one-off character.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: We started with nothing. A taco truck in East Palo Alto.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: Now we own the Sacramento Kings.

jokes.text: We lead the country in online pizza ordering. In fact, a lot of people go to the library just to order pizza online.
jokes.setup: Ben is pitching Pawnee's internet credentials to Gryzzl.
jokes.punchline: His best evidence of Pawnee's internet engagement is that citizens use the public library specifically to order pizza — inadvertently revealing Pawnee's lack of home internet access.
jokes.explanation: Great layered joke — the surface is about internet access, but it also reveals Pawnee's obsession with pizza (a running series joke) AND Ben's earnest-but-inadvertently-damning pitch style. The library detail is the key piece that makes this land — it implies residents don't have home internet but still prioritize pizza delivery.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The library's online pizza ordering system is state-of-the-art. We've seen a 40% increase in digital engagement.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: People are coming to the library just to use our computers now.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's amazing! What are they doing online?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ordering pizza.

jokes.text: Sure, obviously, we're no Akron. I mean, we're more like Dayton. But with your help, we can become Toledo.
jokes.setup: Gryzzl says they're focused on bigger cities like Shreveport and Akron.
jokes.punchline: Ben's aspirational pitch ceiling is Toledo — treating Toledo as a dream destination is both self-deprecating and absurdly modest.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Midwest self-deprecation. The joke works on multiple levels: it satirizes Pawnee's smallness, Ben's earnest pitch style, and the absurdity of aspiring to Toledo. The three-city escalation (Akron → Dayton → Toledo) has perfect comedic rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: We have aspirational goals. We want to be like Columbus, Ohio.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Or failing that, Cleveland.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Or Toledo.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Honestly, we'd settle for Youngstown.

jokes.text: We don't like to say the word 'no'... No. ...at this company.
jokes.setup: The Gryzzl employee begins explaining their company philosophy of avoiding the word 'no.'
jokes.punchline: Ben interjects with a flat 'No' in the exact pause before the explanation is complete.
jokes.explanation: Precision timing comedy. The structure is nearly perfect — the employee's speech has a natural pause, Ben fills it with exactly the word being forbidden, and the employee finishes the sentence as if nothing happened. The follow-up 'How is that better?' grounds it. This is Ben at his deadpan best. Rewatch bonus for the timing.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: We don't say 'no' because it's counterproductive.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: We say 'nah, bro' instead.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: It's the same thing.

jokes.text: 'Nah, bro.' How is that better?
jokes.setup: Gryzzl employee says they replace 'no' with 'Nah, bro' to keep things positive.
jokes.punchline: Ben's genuine confusion — 'How is that better?' — skewers Silicon Valley corporate speak culture.
jokes.explanation: Good follow-through on the previous joke. Ben's bewildered 'How is that better?' is the straight man reaction that grounds the absurdist tech-bro behavior. Short and effective.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, wow, this is... this is really something. The way you've, uh, crafted this... piece. It's very... wooden. And the, the joinery here is so... joinery-like. You can really tell you spent time on the... the whole thing.

jokes.text: Dwayne 'The Rock' Swanson.
jokes.setup: Ron has just been found upstairs where he's been secretly remodeling the entire third floor.
jokes.punchline: Someone greets him as 'Dwayne The Rock Swanson' — a nickname combining Dwayne 'The Rock' Johnson with Ron Swanson, both hyper-masculine archetypal figures.
jokes.explanation: Quick, affectionate nickname joke. The combination of The Rock and Ron Swanson is apt and funny — both are maximally masculine, both are named Ron/Dwayne in an era of action star overlap. Works as a quick character gag.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: We need these chairs faster, Ron. Can you expedite the order?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, any competent person would simply contact Gustafson. He's a Swedish furniture maker from the 1970s. Everybody knows that.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I don't know who that is.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Exactly. Your incompetence is showing again.

jokes.text: All right, I can't keep this facade up any longer. I need a favor.
jokes.setup: Ron has been described as doing extensive, meticulous renovation work on the third floor and is shown admiring the beautiful wood paneling.
jokes.punchline: The 'facade' he can't keep up isn't emotional — it's his pretense of not needing anything. He immediately pivots to asking for help, deflating any notion of Ron vulnerability.
jokes.explanation: Mild character comedy misdirect. The setup implies a rare emotional breakthrough from Ron; the joke is that his 'facade' is just his standard stoicism around needing a favor. Not his sharpest bit but consistent with the character.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, please, I need your help. I'm in a really tight spot financially.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Tom, you need to learn to live within your means. I've always said: never spend money you don't have.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I know, but—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: In fact, I have never spent a dollar I didn't have. Because I always have all my dollars.

jokes.text: Who do you think I am, Thomas Hucker?
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron to rush the chairs he's making. Ron says he was told he had until July.
jokes.punchline: Ron rhetorically asks 'Who do you think I am, Thomas Hucker?' — a fictional character (presumably known for shoddy/rushed work) that only Ron would reference as an insult to his craftsmanship.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron Swanson joke. The comedy is entirely in the specificity — 'Thomas Hucker' is a completely invented craftsman with apparently terrible standards, known only to Ron. The joke implies Ron exists in a parallel universe of woodworking lore the audience isn't privy to. Perfect character integration — this joke is completely impossible to imagine coming from any other character on television.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I had this poster of Rebecca in my childhood bedroom. It was actually just a photo of her dunking on Michael Jordan, but I had Photoshopped her face onto Michael Jordan's body.

jokes.text: Please, Ron? I've never asked you for anything today.
jokes.setup: Tom is begging Ron to speed up his chair-making.
jokes.punchline: Tom's plea that he's 'never asked for anything today' (not 'ever' — just today) inadvertently confesses to his constant demanding nature.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's sharpest jokes. The substitution of 'today' for 'ever' in a stock pleading phrase is minimal but devastating as character comedy. It's entirely Tom that his most passionate appeal inadvertently reveals he asks for things constantly. Extremely quotable and reusable in daily life. Perfect economy — the joke is exactly one word different from the cliché.

dialogue.line: Massive understatement from government bureaucrat

jokes.text: I made a poster of you by blowing up your picture from the National Parks newsletter. I cut out your face and made it look like you were dunking over Charles Barkley.
jokes.setup: Leslie meets Liam Bonneville and Rebecca Varuvian, her government hero role models.
jokes.punchline: Her childhood 'poster' of a National Parks bureaucrat was a DIY collage of the newsletter photo dunking over Charles Barkley — the specific visual is perfectly absurd and character-specific.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant character comedy. Only Leslie Knope would have a childhood poster of a National Parks administrator AND choose to make her heroic by Photoshopping her into a basketball dunk. The Charles Barkley specificity is perfect — he's large and imposing, making the bureaucrat's triumph more absurd. This is the quintessential Leslie joke: obsessive fandom directed at the most niche possible target.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I had the most amazing lunch with these incredible heroes, and I documented every single moment. I have seventeen binders full of photos, receipts, and detailed notes about their sandwich choices.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Did you get their names?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Names? Of course I got their names! They're in binders two through four, cross-referenced alphabetically and by lunch date.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: I mean, did you get their *real* names? Because the guys you had lunch with were the Grant Brothers, and Grant is their last name.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God.

jokes.text: It wasn't bad. / Liam's being withholding as usual. That proposal was brilliantly written.
jokes.setup: Liam Bonneville, the 'resident bad boy' of the Interior Department, reads Leslie's proposal.
jokes.punchline: His damning-with-faint-praise 'It wasn't bad' is revealed by Rebecca to be the highest praise he ever gives — subverting the expectation of a cool bureaucratic bad boy.
jokes.explanation: Good payoff for the 'resident bad boy' setup. The joke is that the Interior's 'bad boy' is actually just emotionally withholding, not edgy in any conventional sense. Rebecca's immediate translation of his insult into high praise is the key comedic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Michelle Obama is from Chicago. Which is a city. In Illinois. A state.

jokes.text: Rebecca Varuvian. Yes? Nothing.
jokes.setup: Leslie gets a chance to speak to her idol Rebecca Varuvian one-on-one.
jokes.punchline: Leslie calls her name, and when Varuvian responds, Leslie just says 'Nothing' — she wanted to say her name out loud but had no actual message. Pure fan-brain.
jokes.explanation: Perfect three-word joke. Leslie calls out the name just to hear herself say it — a brilliant piece of character writing. The economy is nearly perfect (name-response-'nothing') and the beat lands on pure Leslie fangirl energy. Highly relatable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, yes! Yes to everything! Yes to the sun, yes to the moon, yes to all the stars in the sky!

dialogue.speaker: Michelle Obama
dialogue.line: ...I just asked if you wanted coffee.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: YES TO COFFEE! YES TO THIS ENTIRE DIMENSION!

jokes.text: Are you nodding because you agree with me? Yes. I do agree with you. I agree with you on all things. Throughout history. Until the end of time, forever.
jokes.setup: Michelle Obama says Pawnee needs passionate people for national parks.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's agreement escalates from normal assent to declaring eternal cosmic agreement 'throughout history, until the end of time, forever' — fangirl overwhelm expressed through temporal hyperbole.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie Knope escalation joke. The three-part temporal escalation ('throughout history / until the end of time / forever') is metrically perfect and captures her specific brand of overwhelmed reverence. The joke works because it's both funny and completely true to who she is — she would genuinely mean every word of this while knowing it sounds insane.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my God, oh my God, oh my God! Hi! I'm Leslie Knope. I work in the Parks Department. I just want to say that you are an inspiration to me and to women everywhere, and I am literally shaking right now because I'm meeting you and I can't control my volume and I know I'm being too loud but I literally cannot stop talking!

jokes.text: Whoa! That's really, really incredible! Great work! I'm sorry I'm talking so loud! I'm getting louder and now I can't stop! My apologies!
jokes.setup: Michelle Obama describes integrating Let's Move into National Parks.
jokes.punchline: Leslie loses control of her volume, acknowledges it in real time, tries to apologize but keeps getting louder — a physical/vocal escalation she's powerless to stop.
jokes.explanation: This is Amy Poehler-specific physical/verbal escalation comedy at its best. The self-awareness ('I'm getting louder and now I can't stop') combined with continued inability to stop is the essence of cringe comedy — she sees the problem, can't fix it, and apologizes into a louder register. Highly performative joke that requires a great actress to land.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Dude, you're gonna ride that down the hill!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not!

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Come on, man, it'll be awesome!

jokes.text: Can I high-five you?
jokes.setup: Leslie is wrapping up her overwhelmed response to Michelle Obama.
jokes.punchline: After a full meltdown of volume and reverence, Leslie's most dignified closing move is to ask for a high-five — and Michelle Obama grants it.
jokes.explanation: Nice capper to the Michelle Obama sequence. The high-five request is perfectly Leslie — it's the most earnest, unguarded gesture available, and the fact that FLOTUS accepts it is the show's warm-hearted payoff. Not a complex joke but well-placed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh, I met Michelle Obama the other day.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: You what? Wait, you MET Michelle Obama? Like, the First Lady? And you're just casually mentioning this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Yeah, she came through Pawnee for an event.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie, that's huge! Why are you acting like you're telling me about a trip to the grocery store?

jokes.text: Wow! Look at it go! I mean, I knew it would go down, but not that fast! / I thought he was gonna be on it. Yeah. Anyway.
jokes.setup: Andy has apparently set up some kind of stunt or rolling object in San Francisco (likely a wheel of cheese or similar rolling object on a steep hill), having told Leslie to trust him.
jokes.punchline: Whatever Andy sent down the hill went extremely fast — and he wasn't riding it, just watching. Leslie's deadpan 'Yeah. Anyway.' dismisses the whole enterprise.
jokes.explanation: Visual gag that plays better on screen than in transcript. The comedy is in the deflation — Andy's big plan is just to watch something roll down a hill, and 'Yeah. Anyway.' is Leslie doing triage. Rewatch bonus for the visual.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm sorry, but Michelle Obama didn't help me navigate the Parks Department budget process. That obscure bureaucrat did.

jokes.text: This is not government work. As such, I treat it with care and attention.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron to speed up the chairs.
jokes.punchline: Ron explains he's going slowly precisely BECAUSE it's not government work — inverting the expectation that non-government means faster/easier.
jokes.explanation: Quintessential Ron Swanson line. The inversion of expected logic (private work = sloppier? No — for Ron, private work gets his best effort while government work gets minimum effort) is character-specific satire of libertarian philosophy. The joke is simultaneously a character beat and a political position statement. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, can you work any faster on those chairs?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I could, but then they'd be made by the government.

jokes.text: No. Can't I just stay in the back and spit in people's food like we planned?
jokes.setup: Tom tells April she'll be handling service at the restaurant.
jokes.punchline: April's preferred job assignment is food sabotage, presented as a mutually agreed-upon plan.
jokes.explanation: Classic April darkness. The 'like we planned' is the key word — it implies Tom agreed to this, which is both absurd and somehow believable. April's deadpan expectation of getting to commit food sabotage as part of her job duties is perfectly in character. Short and sharp.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: April, can you handle the catering for the event?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Already done. I poisoned the potato salad.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What? Why would you do that?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You said to make sure nobody eats the food. I thought this was the most efficient way.

jokes.text: The sawdust from Ron's chairs is everywhere. My sinuses are on the fritz, and smell is 90% of taste! Maybe 95!
jokes.setup: Craig, the wine taster, is complaining about the prep chaos.
jokes.punchline: His complaint escalates from reasonable (sawdust in sinuses) to hysterical (correcting himself upward on the percentage in real time: '90%! Maybe 95!')
jokes.explanation: Good Craig moment. The live self-correction upward ('90%! Maybe 95!') is the key comedic beat — his anxiety escalates his claims in real time. Captures Craig's specific brand of passionate over-reaction to every minor inconvenience.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Sawdust is affecting all my senses. My eyes are 60% sawdust. My lungs are 70% sawdust.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Actually, my lungs are 80% sawdust now.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: My brain is 90% sawdust.

jokes.text: Fine, but if he raises his voice once, once, I'm out.
jokes.setup: Tom pairs Donna with Craig for wine tasting.
jokes.punchline: Donna's condition is that Craig not raise his voice — but Craig just said 'Maybe 95!' at full volume, and Craig yelling is essentially his defining characteristic.
jokes.explanation: Functional running-gag setup — Craig always yells, so Donna's condition is doomed from the start. Not a complex joke but correctly sets up their dynamic for the wine tasting scene.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I'll work with you, Craig.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Really? That's great! What do you need me to do?

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Just one thing: stop yelling.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: I'M NOT YELLING!

jokes.text: Please don't stick to that policy.
jokes.setup: Donna says she's leaving if Craig raises his voice once.
jokes.punchline: Tom immediately begs her not to honor her own stated policy, knowing Craig is incapable of not yelling.
jokes.explanation: Quick follow-through joke. Tom's resigned awareness that Craig's yelling is inevitable makes this land. Great economy — four words that say everything.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why do all the pictures on menus look so awful?

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: The cameras are bad. And the food is bad. So when you combine bad cameras with bad food, you get bad pictures.

jokes.text: What is this, a rotten grapefruit? No, it's my dog's rectum.
jokes.setup: The restaurant menus have been accidentally printed with photos from Larry's flash drive.
jokes.punchline: The mystery food image is revealed to be Larry's dog's rectum — the specificity of it being a diseased pet anus on a restaurant menu is gloriously horrible.
jokes.explanation: The 'rotten grapefruit/dog rectum' reveal is a great setup-punchline. The beat of Tom genuinely trying to identify the food item before learning the truth is well-constructed. Larry's hapless explanation ('Lord Sheldon has a growth') makes it worse in the best way. The escalating detail — wrong flash drive, vet photos, dog's rectum, restaurant menu — is perfectly Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I was trying to take pictures of my dog for the Christmas card, but I got some... angles... that weren't ideal for a family photo.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Why would you show those to anyone?

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Well, I printed some of them by accident and they ended up at the printer, and then somehow they got mixed in with the menus for the Italian place downstairs.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Jerry, that's— those are dog rectums on restaurant menus.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I know! And it was Italian food, which makes it even worse because now people are going to associate those images with their meal.

jokes.text: Lord Sheldon has a growth, so we're sending pictures over to the vet. But I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?
jokes.setup: Larry explains why his flash drive had pictures of his dog's rectum.
jokes.punchline: His gentle, self-aware ending question — 'But I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?' — is the understatement of the century, delivered with Larry's signature hapless earnestness.
jokes.explanation: The 'I guess this isn't good for menus, is it?' is a perfect Larry line — his self-deprecation and inability to grasp the scale of the disaster he's caused, delivered with complete sincerity. The dog's name 'Lord Sheldon' is also a great detail.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Larry, you've been making mistakes since before I was born. You've made more mistakes than there are stars in the sky. You're like a mistake-making machine. A mistake factory. A mistake... facility.

jokes.text: This is the worst thing you've ever done. I need you to take all of these dog butt pictures and burn them in the pizza oven.
jokes.setup: Tom is dealing with the menu disaster.
jokes.punchline: Tom's solution to the dog butt menu photos is to burn them in the pizza oven — a dramatic, restaurant-specific form of destruction that makes perfect sense and no sense simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Good escalation from the dog butt disaster. 'Pizza oven' as the instrument of menu-destruction adds a nice specificity. 'The worst thing you've ever done' is also a funny over-statement given Larry's history of worse offenses.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Why'd you reject the chair I made?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The joints weren't tight enough. And the finish was uneven. And it's an eyesore.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: I spent three weeks on that chair.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Then you wasted three weeks. A handmade item should be indistinguishable from a factory-made item, except better. Your chair looks like it was made by someone who just discovered wood.

jokes.text: It was too perfect. It looked machine-made.
jokes.setup: Tom asks Ron why he rejected a finished chair.
jokes.punchline: Ron threw away a chair because it was too perfect — his craftsmanship standard is so high that perfection itself is suspicious, implying it must have been machine-assisted.
jokes.explanation: One of Ron's best jokes this episode. The comedic logic is airtight: Ron's handcraft standards are so human-specific that machine-level perfection is actually a disqualifier. The joke reveals both his absurd pride in imperfection-as-authenticity and his impossible standards simultaneously. Near-perfect economy and completely unique to Ron Swanson as a character.

jokes.text: We could tell them that there's buried treasure in Pawnee, and then, after they give us the free WiFi, we tell them that the treasure was love all along.
jokes.setup: Ben says they need to convince Gryzzl that Pawnee is special to get free WiFi.
jokes.punchline: Andy's plan: con them with fake treasure, then reveal the treasure was metaphorical love — both a grift AND an afterschool special simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant Andy joke. The structure is two-part: a scam (fake treasure) combined with a sincere emotional revelation (love was the treasure). The collision of cynical con-artist plan with heartfelt sentimentality is uniquely Andy — he genuinely thinks this is both clever AND touching. The specificity of timing ('after they give us the WiFi') makes it even better.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My legacy will be the free WiFi I'm providing to this town. In a hundred years, people will remember me for bringing high-speed internet to Pawnee.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Children will study my contribution to society. They'll say, 'Ben Wyatt connected us all.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: And they'll use it to watch cat videos and pictures of Chrissy Teigen's butt.

jokes.text: Every time someone in Pawnee clicks through a slideshow of American Music Award red carpet sideboob fails, they'll say, 'Thank you, Ben Wyatt.'
jokes.setup: Ben is passionately arguing for free WiFi for Pawnee citizens.
jokes.punchline: His vision of how Pawnee citizens will honor him is not for civic infrastructure use but specifically for celebrity sideboob slideshow access.
jokes.explanation: Good joke that uses Ben's nerdiness and Pawnee's unsophisticated internet habits as a comedic pairing. 'AMA red carpet sideboob fails' is the perfect specific internet trash content. Ben's complete sincerity about his legacy being this makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, are you guys playing my other games too?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Because I've got this one where you're a sentient bottle of ranch dressing and you have to solve crimes.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's called 'CSI: Salad Dressing.'

jokes.text: Are they throwing dirt into a fan? The key is, you have to throw the dirt into the back of the fan.
jokes.setup: Ben discovers the Gryzzl employees are playing Cones of Dunshire AND throwing dirt into a fan.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately has expert-level opinions on dirt-fan-throwing technique, revealing he invented this game too (or played it enough to have strong opinions).
jokes.explanation: Great Ben/nerd-game joke. Ben's immediate pivot to technical expertise on dirt-fan-throwing (while shocked at seeing it) implies he invented this childlike activity too. Or just that he somehow has strong opinions about it. The specificity of 'the back of the fan' is the key comedic detail.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The key is to cup your hand like you're holding a butterfly, then flick your wrist at the last second so the dirt spirals. It's all in the wrist action.

jokes.text: There can't be an alchemist of the Hinterlands. The Hinterlands is a shadow kingdom that can only sustain a provost or a denier.
jokes.setup: A Gryzzl employee claims to be 'the alchemist of the Hinterlands' in Cones of Dunshire.
jokes.punchline: Ben (the game's inventor) immediately refutes this as a rules violation, citing detailed lore about shadow kingdoms and their political sustainability.
jokes.explanation: This is the Cones of Dunshire lore joke. The comedy is in the completely invented but elaborate specificity — 'shadow kingdom that can only sustain a provost or a denier' sounds like real fantasy game rules. Ben's instant passionate rules correction upon meeting strangers is deeply character-specific. High quotability among fans of the show.

dialogue.speaker: Gryzzl Executive
dialogue.line: So you're the Grand Nagus of Cones of Dunshire?

jokes.text: You wanna be corporal or warrior? Neither. I'm the maverick.
jokes.setup: Ben challenges the Gryzzl team to a Cones of Dunshire game.
jokes.punchline: Offered a choice of standard roles, Ben rejects both and declares himself 'the maverick' — a role presumably he invented as the game's architect.
jokes.explanation: Ben declaring himself 'the maverick' is great — it's simultaneously nerdy (a self-created special role in your own board game) and unexpectedly cool. The word 'maverick' is funny in this context because it's so out of place in board game terminology.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Actually, it's called 'Cones of Dunshire,' and it's a highly sophisticated strategy game with multiple levels of gameplay mechanics, including resource management, tactical positioning, and a unique cone-based economy system.

jokes.text: By using the Leslie Knope Seamless Merger Super System, patent pending...
jokes.setup: Leslie is presenting her plan for the Pawnee-Eagleton merger at a conference.
jokes.punchline: 'Patent pending' on a government merger management plan — Leslie has trademarked a bureaucratic process as if it were an invention.
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie branding joke. Naming and trademarking her merger system is perfectly Leslie — her inability to do anything without branding it is a core character trait. 'Patent pending' is the killer detail.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, those aren't my only options? I choose Maverick.

jokes.text: You know when it was completed? Last month.
jokes.setup: A bureaucrat challenges Leslie's 6-12 month merger timeline, saying he oversaw the Wesham-Southborough merger of 2004.
jokes.punchline: A merger started in 2004 was just completed last month — meaning it took roughly 10 years — completely validating his warning about Leslie's overconfidence.
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke about government inefficiency. The beat of Leslie asking 'When was it completed?' expecting a quick turnaround, then the decade-long answer, is well-structured. Works both as a character beat (humbling Leslie's overconfidence) and a broader satire of government bureaucracy.

jokes.text: You lost your cityhood?
jokes.setup: The bureaucrat explains his hometown was absorbed into unincorporated territory due to mismanaged merger.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horror at 'losing cityhood' — her reaction treating this as the worst possible fate that could befall a community — is played as genuine tragedy, which is funny given the niche nature of municipal governance.
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie reaction beat. For most people, 'unincorporated territory' is an abstract bureaucratic concept; for Leslie it's an existential horror. Her three-word reaction packages the joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Rebecca
dialogue.line: When we merged with Eagleton, we lost all our municipal autonomy. It was a disaster.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what? You lost your municipal status? That's... that's the worst thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: That's a bold flavor. Fruity. A little earthy. Which is it? Fruity or earthy? It can't be both, they're mutually exclusive!
jokes.setup: Craig and Donna are wine tasting together.
jokes.punchline: Craig snaps at Donna's tasting notes with pedantic hostility — wine tasting descriptors 'fruity' and 'earthy' coexisting is apparently an unacceptable paradox to him.
jokes.explanation: Craig having strong opinions about wine descriptor logic is a good niche joke. 'Mutually exclusive!' is the key beat — the word is so technically precise for such a petty complaint. The cringe element is that he's attacking his partner before the restaurant even opens.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: Fruity? FRUITY?! That wine is a symphony of oak-aged complexity with notes of blackberry, plum, and a whisper of vanilla that you're reducing to the word 'fruity'?!

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: And 'earthy'? EARTHY?! Do you know how many terroirs, how many microclimates, how many generations of winemakers' blood, sweat, and tears went into this vintage, and you're just gonna hit me with 'earthy'?!

jokes.text: Oh, no! You do not come at me like that. I'm sorry. I don't know who I am anymore. A man without a palate isn't a man. I love you, Donna.
jokes.setup: Donna fires back at Craig's wine criticism.
jokes.punchline: Craig's emotional arc goes from aggressive confrontation to existential crisis to declaration of love for Donna in about four sentences — the escalation speed is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Craig escalation. The breakdown from aggression → crisis → love declaration is perfectly structured and captures Craig's defining trait: maximum emotional intensity at all times, in all directions. 'A man without a palate isn't a man' is a fantastic absurd aphorism. 'I love you, Donna' as the endpoint is both funny and weirdly touching.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: My palate has betrayed me. I don't know who I am anymore.

jokes.text: We're having a moment, you monster!
jokes.setup: Tom interrupts Craig and Donna's moment to remind them there are customers waiting.
jokes.punchline: Craig calling Tom a 'monster' for interrupting their emotional breakthrough mid-restaurant-crisis is perfectly Craig.
jokes.explanation: Quick, effective capper to the Craig/Donna wine scene. 'You monster!' for what is essentially a reasonable request in a crisis is Craig in concentrated form. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Craig, Donna, what are you two doing?

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: We're having a moment. We bonded over a wine crisis.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: A wine crisis? What happened?

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: That's between us. Some things are sacred.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: We drank a bottle of wine that was meant for the event.

dialogue.speaker: Craig
dialogue.line: And we would do it again! You can't put a price on that kind of connection!

jokes.text: You've always been like a grandpa to me.
jokes.setup: Tom is trying to flatter Ron into lowering his chair-making standards.
jokes.punchline: Tom calls Ron a 'grandpa' figure as a compliment — meant warmly but also slightly insulting, and absolutely not how Ron wants to be seen.
jokes.explanation: Mild Tom/Ron dynamic joke. The 'grandpa' description is both a compliment and an unintentional insult, which is very Tom. Not one of the sharper jokes but earns its place in their scene.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Ron, I have to say, your work ethic is incredible. You never take a day off, you're always here early, you stay late. You're like the least lazy person I've ever met. You're basically the opposite of old.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Thank you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Wait, no, I meant... you're like the opposite of... I meant you're not old.

jokes.text: I play an action card to build a Belltower inside your Citadel. / My shaman casts a Toyber spell on your prosperity tile.
jokes.setup: Ben is playing Cones of Dunshire against Gryzzl employees.
jokes.punchline: The elaborate, entirely invented game terminology ('Toyber spell,' 'prosperity tile,' 'Belltower inside your Citadel') is presented with complete earnestness.
jokes.explanation: Background absurdism as the game plays out. 'Toyber spell' is a particularly funny invented word. These moments work as ambient comedy reinforcing the joke that this is a real, complex game people have mastered.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Whoa, whoa, whoa! Everyone stop! That's good luck!

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Breaking glass at the opening of a restaurant? That means... prosperity and success for seven years.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: It's an old... it's an old Turkish tradition.

jokes.text: You're a smart guy. You've clearly picked up some flashy tricks. But you made one crucial mistake. You forgot about the essence of the game. It's about the cones.
jokes.setup: Ben has been behind in Cones of Dunshire but is about to make a comeback.
jokes.punchline: 'It's about the cones.' — delivered with complete seriousness as a profound game philosophy, when the premise (a game about cones) is inherently absurd.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'It's about the cones' is delivered with the gravity of a profound life lesson, but it's about literal cones in a made-up game. The economy is near-perfect — four words that encapsulate Ben's nerd-earnestness. The pause before the reveal and the structure (flashy tricks → essence → cones) is perfectly constructed. Highly quotable and iconic for the show.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: My winning strategy is simple: I play Checkers.

jokes.text: It's about the cones.
jokes.setup: Ben tells his opponent he made a crucial mistake — the opponent has been playing flashy tricks but missed something fundamental.
jokes.punchline: The profound strategic insight Ben delivers is that the game called Cones of Dunshire is, at its core, about the cones.
jokes.explanation: The single best joke in the episode. The setup borrows the language of profound sports wisdom and hustle-culture insight, and the punchline is simply the game's own title. 'It's about the cones' is simultaneously the most obvious statement possible and, delivered in this context with this gravity, a perfect satirical distillation of Ben's nerd intensity. Exceptional economy (three words), perfect structure (extended dramatic setup → anticlimactic tautological payoff), completely character-specific, and genuinely profound in its own absurdist way. Extremely quotable and rewatch-worthy. This is the Cones of Dunshire saga's best single line.

jokes.text: I move my abbot to the ocean hex, which moves my brinksman to the devil's lair, and pushes my farmer, yes, my humble farmer, directly into the central cone.
jokes.setup: Ben executes his winning move in Cones of Dunshire.
jokes.punchline: The winning move involves: an abbot, an ocean hex, a brinksman, the devil's lair, and a 'humble farmer' — the escalating absurdity of the game pieces, plus the tender pause on 'yes, my humble farmer' as if it's the hero of a great story.
jokes.explanation: Excellent comedy of invented complexity. 'Yes, my humble farmer' is the emotional peak — Ben giving genuine dramatic weight to a made-up game piece. The cascade of nonsense game terms delivers accumulating absurdist laughs, and the farmer callback inverts the expectation (you'd expect the abbot or warrior to be the hero).

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, so if Ben won the game, does that mean Ben owns the company now?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What? No, Andy, it's just a game.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: But you won. Doesn't the winner own everything?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Andy, that's not how this works.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So I've been playing board games wrong my whole life?

jokes.text: Yeah, man! We did it! This whole company is ours! / Oh, no, it's not. That's mine. That's mine. It's all mine.
jokes.setup: Ben wins the Cones of Dunshire game.
jokes.punchline: Andy celebrates as if they jointly won the company; Ben immediately clarifies that the prize is entirely his — gently but firmly.
jokes.explanation: Good dynamic beat between Andy and Ben. Andy's assumption that he's a co-winner despite having no role in the game is very Andy, and Ben's gentle but repeated 'That's mine' is endearing. The triple 'That's mine. That's mine. It's all mine.' has good rhythm.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Okay, pasta types. Penne, rigatoni, fettuccine, linguine, spaghetti, ravioli, macaroni, lasagna, ziti, farfalle, tortellini, angel hair, bow tie, Ferrari, Lamborghini, Maserati, rigatoni, pappardelle.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: April, those last three are cars.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They're Italian.

jokes.text: Hello. Welcome to Tom's Bistro. Today we have spaghetti, linguine, fettuccine, ravioli, rigatoni, bucatini, lasagna. / Could you repeat that? / Spaghetti, linguine, fettuccine, ravioli, rigatoni, Ferrari, Lamborghini, bucatini, lasagna.
jokes.setup: April is reciting the menu from memory after the dog-butt menus were destroyed.
jokes.punchline: On her second recitation, Italian car brands (Ferrari, Lamborghini) have slipped into the pasta list — April either got confused or stopped caring.
jokes.explanation: Brilliant joke. The setup is April performing the menu correctly; the punchline is that Italian car brands have snuck into the second recitation. The joke works because: (1) Ferrari and Lamborghini genuinely sound like pasta names, (2) April's complete deadpan delivery implies she either doesn't notice or doesn't care, (3) the customer asking for a repeat is what creates the opportunity. The structural elegance of needing a second recitation to reveal the corruption is beautiful. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Customer
dialogue.line: Do you have a menu?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We have menus, but they're all sticky, and one of them has a bite taken out of it. Also, our cook is passed out in the walk-in freezer, so you can order whatever you want, but we're only capable of making eggs and also we're out of eggs.

jokes.text: We had to throw our menus away because they are covered with pictures of Larry's dog's rectum.
jokes.setup: A customer asks to see a menu.
jokes.punchline: April explains the situation with total clinical matter-of-factness — no embarrassment, no softening.
jokes.explanation: April delivers the dog butt explanation with perfect detachment. The callback lands because 'Larry's dog's rectum' has now been established as a known quantity. Her complete lack of embarrassment is the joke — she treats this as a perfectly reasonable answer.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: I have great news! My dog is finally going to be okay. The vet said his anal gland infection is completely cleared up.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: That's wonderful, Larry.

dialogue.speaker: Larry
dialogue.line: Yeah, no more pus. The swelling has gone down significantly. His butthole looks almost normal now.

jokes.text: Great news. Lord Sheldon's gonna make it. Yeah. We just have to apply a salve to his anus every hour for the rest of his life, but...
jokes.setup: The opening night is in chaos and there's a customer at the table.
jokes.punchline: Larry chooses this moment to share the good news about his dog's prognosis — including the hourly anus salve detail — to a table of diners.
jokes.explanation: Perfect escalation of the Lord Sheldon running gag. Larry sharing detailed anus treatment protocols with restaurant diners is cringe comedy gold. The 'Great news!' opener makes it even worse — he's framing dog anus medical care as a dinner conversation highlight. The dangling 'but...' implies even he knows this is inappropriate, but not enough to stop.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: This place is a disaster. The food is terrible, the service is nonexistent, and frankly, I've seen better ambiance in a hospital cafeteria. And that's saying something.

jokes.text: Sir, were you sitting in that chair? Yes. Yes, I was. Why? No reason. Let's go.
jokes.setup: Mitch, the investor, has just pulled out of Tom's Bistro after seeing the chaos. He stands to leave.
jokes.punchline: Ron asks if Mitch was sitting in the chair — implying it was one of Ron's rejected 'imperfect' chairs — then immediately says 'No reason' and lets him leave. The implication is the chair was defective and Ron is relieved the investor is no longer sitting in it.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's cleverest structural jokes. It requires the audience to have been paying attention to the chairs subplot — Ron asking about the chair, then saying 'No reason,' implies the chair would have collapsed or was otherwise dangerous. The callback layers add rich meaning. Ron's 'No reason' delivered in his deadpan is perfect. Rewatch bonus for the implication.

jokes.text: I mean, it's all over the Internet. Austin, Charlotte, San Diego. I mean, people are playing with my cones, babe.
jokes.setup: Ben is explaining to Leslie that Cones of Dunshire has spread virally.
jokes.punchline: 'People are playing with my cones, babe' — the sentence means something innocent but sounds inadvertently suggestive, and Ben's complete sincerity makes it funnier.
jokes.explanation: Mild double-entendre that works because of Ben's complete earnestness. Not the most sophisticated comedy but the innocence with which he delivers 'playing with my cones' gets a genuine laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: My childhood strategy was actively ruining fun for others.

jokes.text: And despite what my pocket square says, I'm not a billionaire.
jokes.setup: Tom is confessing the financial reality of losing his investor and having to spend his own money.
jokes.punchline: His self-presentation (pocket square) communicates billionaire status; his actual financial situation does not — and he's aware of this gap.
jokes.explanation: Great Tom joke. The pocket square as a semiotic claim to wealth is very specific to this character. The self-aware admission that his look overclaims his financial status while maintaining the pocket square anyway is perfect Tom Haverford characterization. Great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not gonna lie to you. I'm thinking about quitting. But not because I don't like it here. It's purely ego-driven. I just want to see if I can do something else and be successful at it. You know what I mean?

jokes.text: Really? I love quitting. When I was a kid and things didn't go my way, I would just take my ball and go home. That's better than winning, 'cause then, your friends can't play anymore!
jokes.setup: Ron says he believes you should never start a job you don't intend to finish.
jokes.punchline: Tom reveals his childhood philosophy was taking his ball home specifically to deprive friends of the game — framing this as superior to winning.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom joke. The surprising twist is that he frames 'taking your ball home' not as childish retreat but as a superior strategy — because it denies others the ability to keep playing. The petty logic is perfectly Tom: even his childhood failures were about maintaining control. 'That's better than winning, 'cause then your friends can't play anymore!' is a highly quotable line.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You're doing great, Tom. I'm proud of you.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Really? Thanks, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You've shown real growth. Those chairs you ordered for the office? Perfect choice.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I wanted the department to have the best.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I received the invoice today. Seventy-three thousand dollars.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You are now personally responsible for a debt of seventy-three thousand dollars. I regret my earlier praise.

jokes.text: Well, I hate doing work, but I love being flattered, so maybe I'll give it another try.
jokes.setup: Ron has told Tom he should give the restaurant another shot because he's smart and talented.
jokes.punchline: Tom explicitly parses his decision-making: hatred of work vs. love of flattery, concluding the flattery wins — an honest if unflattering self-assessment.
jokes.explanation: Another great Tom self-awareness joke. The explicit two-factor decision matrix (hates work / loves flattery) is a perfect character distillation. 'So maybe I'll give it another try' as the conclusion to this calculus is both funny and somehow charming. Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I wanted to take you somewhere really special, Leslie. Somewhere that means something to me.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Aww, Ben, that's so sweet!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, so I was thinking about how Yoda is actually 900 years old and—wait, no, sorry. Where was I?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You were being romantic?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Right, yes. I love you and you mean everything to me.

jokes.text: Because you currently owe me $16,000. For the wood.
jokes.setup: Ron encourages Tom to keep going with the restaurant. Tom thanks him, calling it a 'smart move.'
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals his encouragement was financially motivated — Tom owes him $16,000 for the wood in the chairs. The warmth was a debt collection strategy.
jokes.explanation: Classic misdirection with a Ron-specific punchline. We've just had what appears to be a warm mentor moment between Ron and Tom; the reveal that it was debt-motivated completely recontextualizes the exchange in a way that's both funny and entirely consistent with Ron's character. 'For the wood.' as a separate beat lands beautifully.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, yes, hello! I'm calling about the position... Oh my god, I'm sorry, I need to calm down. I'm just so excited about this opportunity that I literally cannot control the volume and cadence of my voice right now.

jokes.text: Wait. I'm on Endor. / These are the redwoods George Lucas used to create the forest moon of Endor. Sorry, that's not why we're here. Let's go.
jokes.setup: Ben takes Leslie somewhere in the San Francisco area.
jokes.punchline: Ben has a Star Wars recognition moment — then immediately redirects because he knows he's supposed to be doing something more important.
jokes.explanation: Good Ben nerd joke. The self-correction ('Sorry, that's not why we're here') is the key beat — he can't fully suppress the Star Wars excitement but knows this isn't the moment. Shows growth as a character while maintaining his defining nerdiness.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I love you! I mean, I love your enthusiasm. Your enthusiastic... I love your... Ben! I'm talking to Ben!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Hi, yes, it's me. I just got very excited about the community garden initiative and I... I may have said something weird.

jokes.text: Smoothly handled, Lester. Yeah. I panicked.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just concluded her chaotic phone call accepting the job.
jokes.punchline: Ben's dry 'Smoothly handled, Lester' and Leslie's complete, earnest agreement — 'Yeah. I panicked.' — is the perfect button on the chaos.
jokes.explanation: Strong button. Ben's sarcasm is perfectly delivered and 'Yeah. I panicked.' from Leslie — not defensive, just matter-of-fact — is the ideal response. Economy is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Jean-Ralphio, I need your help at the restaurant.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: Oh dude, I'm there. What do you need? You need me to... seduce someone? Because I will seduce someone right now.

jokes.text: Did someone call for a party zoo? / All right, so we got a four-way going with my ex, my brother, and this rando? Okay, if that's where the night is going. It's 9:00 in the morning.
jokes.setup: Tom calls in reinforcements for the restaurant opening.
jokes.punchline: Jean-Ralphio arrives, surveys the group, immediately interprets the situation as a sexual arrangement, and is informed it's 9 AM.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Jean-Ralphio entrance. 'Did someone call for a party zoo?' as a self-introduction is strong, but the real joke is the immediate sexual misreading of the gathering and Donna's flat '9:00 in the morning' correction. Character-specific and well-timed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Ron, will you play Duke Silver at the charity event?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Absolutely not. I don't perform. I don't do charity events. I don't do anything that requires me to be around large groups of people who will ask me questions about my personal life.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's just one night, Ron.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: One night is 1,440 minutes of potential human interaction. I'd rather spend those minutes alone with a bottle of scotch and a woodworking project.

jokes.text: Thank you, Andrew. But fun or not, playing music is something I like to keep private, along with my family, my conversations, and my whereabouts at all times.
jokes.setup: Andy invites Ron to perform at the Unity Concert as Duke Silver.
jokes.punchline: Ron declines by listing things he keeps private — escalating from music to family to conversations to 'my whereabouts at all times,' the last item revealing paranoid survivalist tendencies.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron lines. The escalation from reasonable privacy ('music,' 'family') to 'my whereabouts at all times' is a perfect reveal of Ron's libertarian paranoia. The list structure is metrically satisfying and builds to the right payoff. Extremely Ron-specific — the line could not come from any other character on television. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to complete this mission. If you fail to complete this mission, you will have failed at completing this mission. And if you succeed at completing this mission, you will have successfully completed this mission.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: This message will self-destruct in five seconds... or it won't, depending on whether you complete the mission.

jokes.text: Your mission, should you choose to accept it, is to accept the following missions.
jokes.setup: Andy is given leadership of the Unity Concert as a Mission: Impossible-style briefing.
jokes.punchline: The tautological Mission: Impossible parody — the mission is to accept the missions.
jokes.explanation: Great Andy moment. The Mission: Impossible reference applied to community concert planning is funny, but the real joke is that Andy's version of the famous phrase is a logical loop: the mission is to accept missions. It's both dumb and somehow philosophically interesting. Very Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so the official name of our volunteer group is the Pawnee Parks Department Community Outreach Initiative for Environmental Stewardship and Civic Engagement Task Force.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? That's too long. We're gonna need to shorten that.

jokes.text: Their first project will be to come up with a shorter name for the group.
jokes.setup: Andy announces the 'Pawnee-Eagleton Merger Preservation Volunteer Action Squad' needs 2,000 signups.
jokes.punchline: He immediately acknowledges the name is terrible and assigns the group to fix it as their first task.
jokes.explanation: Nicely structured self-aware joke. The name is announced, immediately acknowledged as too long, and the fix is delegated to the group itself. The efficiency of this comedic move — naming the problem and solving it in the same breath — is good writing.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: The volunteer group name is too long.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: We need larger hats to fit more text on them.

jokes.text: You're right, the name is too long, I was picturing bigger hats.
jokes.setup: The name for the volunteer group is agreed to be too long.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's explanation for why she wanted a long name is that she envisioned proportionally larger hats for members — the name length correlates to hat size in her mind.
jokes.explanation: Outstanding Leslie joke. The logic connecting 'long name' to 'bigger hats' is uniquely Leslie — she visualizes community organizations in terms of their ceremonial regalia, and hat size is apparently proportional to the name's length in her mental model. The specificity of 'I was picturing bigger hats' is completely unexpected and totally character-specific. One of the episode's most quotable lines.

dialogue.speaker: Statue inscription
dialogue.line: Here lies Leslie Knope. She died doing what she loved: being faithful to Pawnee.

jokes.text: 'Only a moron would ever live anywhere other than Pawnee, Indiana.' Leslie Knope, multiple occasions.
jokes.setup: Leslie is touched by the statue dedication — until they reveal the inscription, given that she's leaving Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: The chosen quote — perfectly Leslie in its earnestness — becomes accidentally ironic given she just announced she's moving away. 'Multiple occasions' makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural irony. The statue quote is absolutely something Leslie would say and believe — and the timing of the reveal (immediately after she announces she's leaving) creates perfect comedic and emotional resonance. 'Multiple occasions' as the attribution is the key word that makes it land — she said this repeatedly with full conviction, and now she's contradicting it. The bittersweet comedy is perfectly Parks & Rec in tone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: "I would never leave Pawnee. This is my home. I belong here."

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Well, that aged well.

jokes.text: I can cut a new plinth with a less ironic inscription.
jokes.setup: The statue quote is revealed to be ironic given Leslie's departure.
jokes.punchline: Ron, ever practical, offers a solution — recut the plinth with something less ironic. His literal problem-solving applied to an emotional moment is perfect Ron.
jokes.explanation: Ron's practical response to what should be an emotional moment is perfectly in character. The offer to 'cut a new plinth' treats the irony as a carpentry problem rather than an existential one. Excellent economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, your tears have created a salt stain on my shirt. Please stop.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't help it, Ron. I'm just so emotional right now.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Crying is for children and people who don't have woodworking to do. I suggest you find a hobby.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's... not helping.

jokes.text: Leslie, don't cry. It's not that great. Doesn't even look like you. / Or actually, you know what? It kinda does.
jokes.setup: Someone tries to comfort Leslie by downplaying the statue.
jokes.punchline: Mid-sentence self-correction — the person realizes the statue actually does look like her, which accidentally makes it worse as a comfort attempt.
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The failed comfort attempt where the correction makes things worse is a well-worn structure, but the specific detail (realizing the statue actually IS a good likeness) makes this version land. The pause between the initial claim and the retraction is key.

dialogue.speaker: Decemberists member
dialogue.line: Your town of Pawnee is truly a beacon of culture and innovation.

dialogue.speaker: Decemberists member
dialogue.line: I mean, where else can you get a waffle topped with bacon and candy corn?

jokes.text: I ordered a small cheeseburger and both the buns were pizzas.
jokes.setup: The Decemberists are performing at the Unity Concert and commenting on Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: The band's most notable experience of Pawnee is a cheeseburger where both buns were replaced with pizzas — a perfect encapsulation of Pawnee's absurd food culture.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. 'Both the buns were pizzas' is a gem of food absurdism that distills Pawnee's food culture — already established across seasons as comically unhealthy — into one perfect image. The matter-of-fact delivery from an indie band member makes it funnier. The specificity of 'both' buns is key. Extremely quotable and works completely out of context.

dialogue.speaker: Jean-Ralphio
dialogue.line: I'm proud of creating legal precedent for double ankle bracelets

jokes.text: The only reason I wouldn't be there is if I got pulled over. For violating my house arrest.
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio is invited to Tom's Bistro opening.
jokes.punchline: His attendance caveat is the possibility of being caught violating an existing house arrest order — delivered as if this is a normal social scheduling conflict.
jokes.explanation: Good Jean-Ralphio character joke. The house arrest reveal is the kind of casual criminal background detail that defines his character. Treated as a mundane scheduling concern rather than a legal crisis.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: We're called 'The Pit' — we do Police covers, but we make them worse on purpose. It's ironic.

dialogue.speaker: Jeremy Jamm
dialogue.line: ♪ Every breath you take, every move you make, every bond you break... ♪

jokes.text: Judge gave me two ankle bracelets. Said it was the first time he ever had to do that. Ja boy's a question on the bar exam! Ya heard!
jokes.setup: Jean-Ralphio has revealed he's on house arrest.
jokes.punchline: He's on house arrest so severe it required two ankle bracelets — a first for the judge — and he's proud enough of this distinction to boast that he's now a bar exam question.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Jean-Ralphio escalation. 'Two ankle bracelets' is already funny; 'the judge said it was the first time he ever had to do that' is better; 'I'm a question on the bar exam' is the perfect absurdist peak. Jean-Ralphio treating this as a source of pride and prestige rather than shame is completely character-specific. 'Ya heard!' is the right punctuation. One of his best moments.

jokes.text: Did someone say 'dental plan'?
jokes.setup: Ben is discussing relocation benefits with Grant — specifically that the dental plan is 'more than fair.'
jokes.punchline: Jamm, an orthodontist-councilman, materializes at the mention of dental care.
jokes.explanation: Good Jamm entrance joke. An orthodontist councilman appearing the moment dental benefits are mentioned is both logical and absurd. The Simpsons-esque timing of being summoned by key words is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, I'm offering you the position of Parks Director. You'd be working with me every day.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Leslie, I appreciate the offer, but I'm not interested.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Not even a little bit? We could accomplish so much together.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: My answer is final. I'm done with government work.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, what if I told you we're getting a new espresso machine? And a waffle bar?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A waffle bar? How many waffles?

jokes.text: Hey, I think we can all agree this concert blows, right? If you guys really wanna see a crowd, you might wanna stop by my secession rally later tonight. That is gonna be off the hook. You ever heard of Warrant? Yeah. There's a cover band right here, that call themselves Cherry Pie.
jokes.setup: Jamm inserts himself into a conversation about relocation packages.
jokes.punchline: Jamm's rival event — a secession rally — features a cover band called Cherry Pie covering the band Warrant, implying he couldn't even book the tribute band's own name.
jokes.explanation: Classic Jamm — his attempted rival event is pathetically small (a cover band covering Warrant) but he's completely sincere about its appeal. The specificity of 'Cherry Pie' as the cover band name (the name of Warrant's most famous song) is a nice music nerd detail.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I'm here because Ron asked me to help with the children's event.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I love children. I want to take them home with me.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: I LOVE children. I want to TAKE them home with me.

jokes.text: What is that? / Just general rock, man. It's gonna be fun. / She's my cherry pie, oh yeah yeah yeah
jokes.setup: Jamm has promised his rally will be great and features Cherry Pie.
jokes.punchline: The actual sound of Cherry Pie playing is immediately audible — and it sounds exactly as bad as expected.
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on Jamm's terrible rally. Works as a confirmation joke — the sound of the band validates the setup. Not particularly sophisticated but functional.

dialogue.speaker: Tammy II
dialogue.line: Ron, if you don't do exactly what I say, I'm going to take all your teakwood and turn it into a birdhouse.

jokes.text: Ginuwine, it is an honor to be breathing the same air as you. No joke. But real talk, we're both men about town being constantly bombarded with party invitations.
jokes.setup: Tom is pitching Ginuwine (the R&B singer) to come to his restaurant opening.
jokes.punchline: Tom establishes profound reverence ('no joke') and then immediately pivots to a transparently self-aggrandizing comparison — positioning himself as Ginuwine's social equal as 'men about town.'
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom character joke. The 'no joke' → immediately making a very debatable claim is perfectly Tom's sycophantic-but-self-aggrandizing social style. 'Men about town' is a funny, slightly dated phrase for the context.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I thought we'd get signed to a major label, go on a world tour, sell out Madison Square Garden. Then I'd get injured during a guitar solo, become a chess master, and we'd break up so I could pursue my true passion: competitive tickling.

jokes.text: Who is this guy? / My friend who's opening a restaurant tonight, and you're going to be there, cousin. Unless you want me to get on stage and talk about how we used to take baths together. How you cried whenever I took away your rubber duckies.
jokes.setup: Donna is trying to get Ginuwine (her famous cousin) to attend Tom's Bistro opening.
jokes.punchline: Donna blackmails her famous cousin with childhood bath stories and rubber duck tears — intimate family leverage deployed with zero hesitation.
jokes.explanation: Good Donna/Ginuwine joke. The blackmail material is perfectly chosen — public revelation of adult R&B star crying over rubber ducks is the right level of embarrassing to be credible. Donna's complete lack of hesitation in deploying this threat is very Donna.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Your performance was so bad, you made someone pee their pants.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's the best compliment I've ever received.

jokes.text: Damn, Donna, why you gotta bring the Quackson Five into this?
jokes.setup: Donna has threatened to reveal his crying over rubber duckies.
jokes.punchline: Ginuwine's nickname for his rubber duck collection is 'the Quackson Five' — a duck-based Jackson Five pun that implies he named and ranked his ducks.
jokes.explanation: The single most purely funny wordplay joke in the episode. 'The Quackson Five' is a perfect name: it's a duck pun on the Jackson Five, it implies the ducks were a named group of exactly five, and it's delivered by Ginuwine (real R&B star) as an indignant protest, which adds a layer of meta-comedy. The name exists in one line, creates an entire backstory, and is immediately understood and loved. 'Why you gotta bring the Quackson Five into this?' is one of the most quotable lines in the episode and possibly the season. Maximum economy — three words do enormous comedic work.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You lost my phone in a ball pit?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was trying to get the blue ones out because they match your eyes, and—

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Wait. You were in a ball pit?

jokes.text: Now if you'll excuse me, there's a booth over there serving something called 'fried sausage quilts,' so I'm going to buy the booth.
jokes.setup: Ron declines Leslie's invitation to move to Chicago with warmth but finality.
jokes.punchline: Ron's pivot is to purchase an entire food booth at the concert because it serves 'fried sausage quilts' — both the food item and his response (buying the booth rather than just ordering) are perfectly Ron.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best Ron moments. 'Fried sausage quilts' is a brilliant invented food — it sounds simultaneously disgusting and appealing, and is exactly the kind of thing a county fair would serve. But the joke's peak is Ron's response: he doesn't say 'I'm going to get some' — he says 'I'm going to buy the booth.' The scale of his food commitment (purchasing the entire vendor) is character-perfect. This is Ron Swanson in three words. Extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I don't want your job, but I also can't believe you didn't offer it to me sooner. I hate this department, but I'd die for it. You're the worst, but you're also the best. I'm leaving, but I'm not going anywhere.

jokes.text: I recalibrated the sights on all the rifles in the shooting gallery. I've had enough fun for one day.
jokes.setup: Ron is at the festival. Diane and his daughter suggest he should have fun.
jokes.punchline: Ron's version of fun is recalibrating rifle sights at a carnival shooting gallery — and he's already satisfied for the day.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Ron character joke. Rifle sight recalibration as a leisure activity, done at a children's carnival, and being 'satisfied for the day' — this is Ron's complete personality in one sentence. The specificity (recalibrating, not just shooting) and the satisfaction (one activity = full day of fun) are both right.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: I need money. Now. Give me money.

jokes.text: Tammy. / What could possibly bring you to a children's performance? Preparing a ritual sacrifice of a newborn?
jokes.setup: Tammy 2 appears unexpectedly at the children's concert.
jokes.punchline: Ron's first instinct to explain her presence at a children's show is ritual infant sacrifice.
jokes.explanation: Good Tammy 2 joke. The dark turn to 'ritual sacrifice of a newborn' as Ron's most plausible explanation for her being near children is a strong character beat. It establishes both how much he despises her and how genuinely diabolical she is in his worldview.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: What'll it be?

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: I'll have a Joan.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: A Joan? I don't know that one.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
dialogue.line: It's equal parts vodka, gin, and regret, with a splash of existential dread.

dialogue.speaker: Bartender
dialogue.line: That's just... depression in a glass.

dialogue.speaker: Joan
