dialogue.line: Exactly. Now make it a double.

jokes.text: No, just trolling for some daddy. Sorry, I pronounced that wrong. I'm trolling for some dad-dy.
jokes.setup: Ron asks Tammy why she's at a children's performance.
jokes.punchline: Tammy's answer is sexual — she's looking for men — delivered as a deliberate mispronunciation-then-correction that makes it unmistakably lewd.
jokes.explanation: Great Tammy 2 wordplay. The pretend mispronunciation correction ('sorry, I said that wrong... dad-DY') is a classic double entendre delivery that makes the intent completely clear while maintaining plausible deniability. The deadpan self-correction sells it.

dialogue.speaker: Barney
dialogue.line: Want to work at my accounting firm?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No.

dialogue.speaker: Barney
dialogue.line: That was fast. I didn't even get to the part about the free coffee.

jokes.text: Diane, why don't you take the girls for some ice cream while I dispose of this sewer-dwelling gutter witch?
jokes.setup: Tammy 2 has appeared and Ron needs to deal with her.
jokes.punchline: Ron instructs his wife to take the kids for ice cream while he 'disposes of' Tammy — framing it as a normal household chore, with 'sewer-dwelling gutter witch' as a perfectly calibrated insult.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Ron insult delivery. 'Sewer-dwelling gutter witch' is a fantastic compound insult — it evokes the right image, escalates through three distinct insulting concepts (sewer-dwelling / gutter / witch), and is delivered with Ron's standard flat affect as if it's a clinical description. The framing of it as a domestic chore ('while I dispose of') makes it funnier. Extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I wish we could get married again.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We could get divorced and then remarry.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's the best idea you've ever had!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I know.

jokes.text: I will defeat you right into my pants.
jokes.setup: Ron threatens to 'defeat' Tammy.
jokes.punchline: Tammy converts Ron's aggressive threat into a sexual invitation in a single sentence, redefining 'defeat' as erotic conquest.
jokes.explanation: Tammy 2 at her best. The four-word punchline 'right into my pants' completely inverts the aggressive tone of the exchange. The economy is exceptional — she doesn't explain or elaborate, just redirects. Highly quotable and captures the Tammy/Ron dynamic perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dr. Saperstein
dialogue.line: This Italian food is exquisite! You know, it reminds me of the authentic cuisine I experienced in Dallas.

jokes.text: And then in the first game, of course, I break my leg. The crowd starts chanting my name, and I give them the thumbs up. And then I go to the hospital, I get really good at chess, I end up beating the computer finally. And then the band just sort of drifts apart.
jokes.setup: Andy tells his old bandmate Burly how he always imagined Mouse Rat breaking up.
jokes.punchline: Andy's imagined band breakup scenario is a chain of completely non-sequitur events: NFL debut → broken leg → thumbs up → chess mastery → band drift. The connection between any of these events is completely Andy-logic.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best character comedy moments. The joke is that Andy has an extremely detailed fantasy breakup scenario that makes no internal logical sense — and he's describing it to an old friend as if sharing a mutual memory. 'I get really good at chess, I end up beating the computer finally' as a step in the band's dissolution is perfect. The wistful sincerity ('That was how I saw it, but...') makes it even better. This is peak Andy Dwyer.

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Can I get a photo with you? I'm a huge fan. I'm going to Instagram this as '#KeepingItLit.'

jokes.text: One kid peed his pants because he didn't want to miss anything. / What? I gave a kid pee-pants? / Yes! / That's why I do what I do.
jokes.setup: April is telling Andy how great his performance was.
jokes.punchline: Andy's measurement of success as a performer is whether he's caused involuntary pants-wetting in the audience — and 'pee-pants' being confirmed is his highest professional achievement.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Andy joke. 'I gave a kid pee-pants?' expressed with reverent wonder, then 'That's why I do what I do' as the artistic manifesto — it's a perfect encapsulation of Andy's childlike worldview. The joke works because it's simultaneously absurd (pee-pants as achievement) and emotionally true (performers want to create unforgettable experiences). Very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You won't.

jokes.text: I hope you like deep-dish pizza, because there's gonna be a lot more of it in Chicago, where we're all gonna be moving.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just told Ben she took the job in Chicago.
jokes.punchline: Ben announces to their group that they're all moving to Chicago, unilaterally — ignoring that no one else was offered or agreed to a job there.
jokes.explanation: Good Ben enthusiasm joke. His immediate collective-we announcement is both sweet (he's excited for Leslie) and absurd (no one agreed to this). The pizza framing is classic Ben food-nerd motivation.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, Leslie, you'd be an excellent coal miner. You have the work ethic, the determination, the complete disregard for your own safety.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ron, that's not a compliment.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It absolutely is. I've never seen someone so willing to sacrifice their body for a cause they believe in. You'd make it maybe three weeks before a cave-in.

jokes.text: I love you, Kay Hanley! (shouted at musician from crowd)
jokes.setup: Kay Hanley of Letters to Cleo is performing at the concert.
jokes.punchline: Andy shouts 'I love you, Kay Hanley!' like an excited fan — he's simultaneously a performer and a completely uncool audience member who shouts at other artists.
jokes.explanation: Light Andy character beat. The cognitive dissonance of Andy as a performer/fan is funny but this is a minor laugh moment rather than a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Leslie's proposal is interesting, but I have some concerns about the feasibility and cost.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: What kind of concerns?

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: Well, for starters, we'd need to allocate significant resources, and I'm not sure the ROI justifies it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: But think about the community impact!

dialogue.speaker: Grant
dialogue.line: I understand, but as government officials, we can't just approve every request that comes through. Speaking of which, I got a letter today asking if the Parks Department could arrange for the Power Rangers to visit Pawnee. Apparently, someone thought that was within our jurisdiction.

jokes.text: Pawnee is cheap and we like it here, and Chicago seems like there's a lot of stuff to do and people, but I like to do nothing with no one. So, thank you and I love you, but no thank you, and I hate you. More I love you.
jokes.setup: Ben is trying to convince the group to move to Chicago.
jokes.punchline: April's rejection speech is a perfectly structured series of contradictions — 'thank you/no thank you,' 'I love you/I hate you/more I love you' — plus the revelation that her ideal life is 'doing nothing with no one.'
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and one of the best April lines of the series. 'I like to do nothing with no one' is the perfect encapsulation of April's anti-social character in six words. The formal speech structure ('thank you and I love you, but no thank you, and I hate you. More I love you.') applies diplomatic language to total emotional chaos. The corrected ending — 'More I love you' — is the perfect beat. This is as character-specific as comedy gets. Extremely quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ed, I'm going to have to let you go. You're just not cutting it here.

dialogue.speaker: Ed
dialogue.line: What? But I've been trying my best!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I know, and I appreciate that, but this just isn't working out.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: Wait, wait, wait. So you're saying I'm not good enough either? Is that what this is about?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Terry, you're not being fired. Ed is being fired.

dialogue.speaker: Terry
dialogue.line: Yeah, but the fact that you even had to fire someone... I feel like maybe I should've seen this coming. Am I next?

jokes.text: Thank you, Pawnee! We have been Bobby Knight Ranger!
jokes.setup: A band is closing their set at the concert.
jokes.punchline: Their band name is 'Bobby Knight Ranger' — a mashup of the Indiana basketball coach Bobby Knight and Night Ranger (80s rock band), making a perfectly Indiana-specific punny band name.
jokes.explanation: Good Pawnee-specific wordplay. 'Bobby Knight Ranger' requires knowing both Indiana basketball and 80s rock but delivers a crisp, satisfying pun when it lands. Economy is high — the joke is entirely in the band name.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: So how do we feed the kids?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Well, we prepare nutritious meals, keep a regular schedule, and make sure they eat vegetables.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Or, hear me out, we let them eat nothing but frozen pizza and candy until they pass out, then we eat their leftovers.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: That's... that's not parenting, Andy.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: It's not NOT parenting.

jokes.text: Super cool to hear Sister Christian that many times in a row!
jokes.setup: Andy is MCing the transition between acts.
jokes.punchline: The implication that Bobby Knight Ranger played 'Sister Christian' (Night Ranger's hit) multiple times in a row — and Andy's cheerful acceptance of this as 'super cool' — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: Good callback to the Bobby Knight Ranger joke. The detail that they played 'Sister Christian' multiple times in a row, and Andy's uncritical enthusiasm about it, is funny. The joke requires the preceding setup.

jokes.text: No! Your father ruined my last business. Why would you bring him here? / Mmm, because you told me to look for VIPs and my daddy is the VI-est P I know.
jokes.setup: Mona-Lisa has brought Dr. Saperstein (her and Jean-Ralphio's father, Tom's nemesis) to the restaurant opening.
jokes.punchline: 'My daddy is the VI-est P I know' — Mona-Lisa's breakdown of 'VIP' into 'VI' and 'P' to argue that her father qualifies is a fun piece of wordplay that's also characteristically Mona-Lisa logic.
jokes.explanation: Sharp wordplay. 'The VI-est P I know' deconstructs VIP into a superlative-adjective construction ('very important') in a way that's clever and character-specific to Mona-Lisa's self-serving logic.

jokes.text: I came here to see your flourishing business. To see how well you're doing. Wow! You're packed! Can you squeeze me in, or do I need a reservation? 'Cause there's nobody here.
jokes.setup: Dr. Saperstein arrives at Tom's Bistro's after-party and surveys the empty restaurant.
jokes.punchline: Saperstein performs sincere admiration ('You're packed!') and then immediately, flatly states the obvious truth: 'There's nobody here.' — the sarcasm switch thrown in one sentence.
jokes.explanation: Good Saperstein joke. The reversal from performed enthusiasm to flat reality check is sharp. 'You're packed!' followed by ''cause there's nobody here' is a well-timed sarcastic pivot.

jokes.text: This is amazing. How can I ever repay you? / Come work for us at the accounting firm? / Okay. / No, sorry, I can't. / Wow. Shortest one yet.
jokes.setup: Barney has given Ben the copyright to Cones of Dunshire as a gift.
jokes.punchline: Barney immediately pitches Ben on joining the accounting firm; Ben says okay then immediately retracts it; Barney notes it was the 'shortest one yet' — implying he's been asking Ben repeatedly and getting faster rejections each time.
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured running-gag joke. The fact that Barney always asks, that Ben always says a reflexive 'Okay' before catching himself, and that Barney now tracks the response time ('shortest one yet') is delightful. The escalation of the running gag is revealed in a single beat. Near-perfect economy.

jokes.text: I wish I could marry you all over again. / Let's get divorced. That way we can get married again! / Yes! Let's do it. / You want to? Yes! / We should do that, right? Yeah, totally. / We're getting divorced! Yes!
jokes.setup: Andy says he wishes he could marry April again.
jokes.punchline: April's solution to marry again is to get divorced first — and both of them immediately and enthusiastically commit to divorce as a romantic gesture.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. The comedic logic is perfect: divorce as a romantic act to enable a second marriage. The escalating enthusiasm ('You want to? Yes! We should do that, right? Yeah, totally. We're getting divorced! Yes!') reaches a joyful absurd peak. It's also character-perfect — only Andy and April would celebrate their divorce as an act of love. The structural repetition of mutual confirmation builds the joke beautifully.

jokes.text: Except for Liam Hemsworth and Miley Cyrus. I was hoping tonight would be magical enough to get them back together. / Let it go, friend. He's not good enough for her. / And vice-versa!
jokes.setup: Tom is thrilled that nearly everyone he invited came to the opening.
jokes.punchline: Tom's celebrity guest list included trying to engineer a Miley Cyrus/Liam Hemsworth reconciliation via Italian food. Donna's defense of Miley and Leslie's 'and vice-versa!' disagrees with Donna.
jokes.explanation: Good Tom joke — his ambitions for the restaurant extend to celebrity matchmaking. The Leslie/Donna disagreement about who's 'good enough' adds a nice layer. 'And vice-versa!' from Leslie is the best beat.

jokes.text: Excuse me, Miss Hanley? Do you mind if I snap a 'You-ie'? It's what I call selfies of other people.
jokes.setup: Tom is getting photos for his Wall of Fame.
jokes.punchline: Tom has invented 'You-ie' as his term for photographing famous people — a 'selfie' but starring someone else. The neologism is both nonsensical and somehow logical.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Tom neologism. 'You-ie' as a term for selfies of other people (as opposed to a 'selfie' which is of yourself) is the kind of word invention Tom would do and be completely serious about. The explanation ('It's what I call selfies of other people') adds a perfect beat. Very Tom, very quotable.

jokes.text: Everybody turned me down but Larry. / Ouch. Yeah.
jokes.setup: Leslie tried to recruit colleagues for her new Chicago-area team.
jokes.punchline: The only person who agreed to follow her was Larry — and both she and Ben immediately recognize this as a damning data point about the offer's appeal.
jokes.explanation: Clean Larry joke. 'Ouch. Yeah.' from Ben perfectly captures the resignation and shared understanding. The joke works because everyone knows Larry would be the only one desperate enough to say yes, and that his enthusiasm is somehow worse than rejection.

jokes.text: With your courage and small frame, you'd make an excellent coal miner.
jokes.setup: Ron is offering career advice to Leslie as a form of encouragement.
jokes.punchline: His highest compliment for Leslie's skills and attributes is coal mining suitability — citing her 'small frame' as a professional asset.
jokes.explanation: Classic Ron compliment. The coal miner recommendation is simultaneously a non-sequitur and perfectly Ron — physical labor, self-sufficiency, dangerous conditions. Citing her 'small frame' as the qualifying credential is the key specificity. Leslie receiving this as 'very sweet' is the perfect reaction. Only Ron would offer this as encouragement.

jokes.text: Oh, my God. I can have everything I want! Thank you! / I feel like you're not listening to me.
jokes.setup: Ron says 'you can't have everything you want' as a gentle lesson about leaving Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Leslie hears this as permission to have everything she wants, interpreting Ron's philosophical resignation as tactical advice — and Ron immediately recognizes she missed the point.
jokes.explanation: Perfect Leslie/Ron dynamic joke. Ron offers wisdom; Leslie hears permission. Her 'I can have everything I want!' followed by Ron's flat 'I feel like you're not listening to me' is textbook Parks & Rec — Leslie's boundless optimism colliding with Ron's pragmatism. The joke also has emotional depth because her optimism ends up being right.

jokes.text: And by the way, don't think that we are not discussing Duke Silver. When were you going to tell me about that? Unbelievable. I am so furious at you. But I've already forgiven you and you need to teach me how to play the saxophone. Okay, bye.
jokes.setup: Leslie has just discovered Ron is Duke Silver.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's emotional sequence — fury → immediate forgiveness → saxophone lessons request → abrupt goodbye — completes in about ten seconds.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie closing bit. The speed of her emotional arc (outrage → forgiveness → curriculum planning → exit) is pure character comedy. 'I've already forgiven you' delivered while still claiming to be furious captures Leslie's fundamental inability to sustain negative emotions. 'You need to teach me how to play the saxophone. Okay, bye.' as the practical endpoint is perfect.

jokes.text: The financial savings here are enormous. The cost of living is way lower here, and renting the entire third floor of this building would be way cheaper than a much smaller space in Chicago. Pawnee is actually closer to most of the parks in the Midwest region. And, it's got Tom's Bistro, an exciting, new-wave, Italian eatery, that is equal parts Dean Martin and Bruno Mars. But that is just what the Indianapolis Star is saying.
jokes.setup: Leslie pitches Grant on basing the new Midwest bureau in Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Her pitch descends from legitimate geographic and financial arguments into quoting the Indianapolis Star's review of Tom's Bistro as evidence for national parks placement.
jokes.explanation: Good Leslie pitch joke. 'Equal parts Dean Martin and Bruno Mars' is a fun description, and the reveal that this is from the Indianapolis Star (not a national publication) is a nice deflation. The inclusion of a restaurant review in a federal bureau location pitch is quintessential Leslie.

jokes.text: And, it's got Tom's Bistro, an exciting, new-wave, Italian eatery, that is equal parts Dean Martin and Bruno Mars. But that is just what the Indianapolis Star is saying.
jokes.setup: Leslie is pitching Pawnee to Grant as the location for her Midwest bureau.
jokes.punchline: Leslie citing 'Tom's Bistro' as a key selling point for the federal government, then sourcing 'the Indianapolis Star' — implying she pitched Tom's Bistro to the local press as part of her scheme.
jokes.explanation: Good double joke — Leslie using Tom's Bistro as federal location justification is funny, and 'equal parts Dean Martin and Bruno Mars' as a restaurant description (then attributed to the Indianapolis Star) is a nice absurdist detail.

jokes.text: Leslie should stay here. And if you don't agree with us, it's nine against one and we can make you disappear forever. / What? / I said we have free WiFi.
jokes.setup: The Parks team is making the case to Grant for Leslie working from Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: Someone threatens to 'make Grant disappear forever' then immediately walks it back as 'we have free WiFi' — a comedic cover-up that sounds exactly like what it is.
jokes.explanation: Good dark joke. The threat → bad cover story is a classic structure, and 'we have free WiFi' is a funny specific replacement for a disappearance threat. The callback to the Gryzzl WiFi plot is a nice bonus.

jokes.text: I'll run this up the flagpole. Also, can you bring back Power Rangers? I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done.
jokes.setup: Grant agrees to consider Pawnee as the bureau location.
jokes.punchline: Leslie tacks on a Power Rangers revival request — to a National Parks Service official — as if federal importance is general enough to cover entertainment IP.
jokes.explanation: Strong Leslie joke. 'I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done' is particularly good — her vague sense that Grant has undifferentiated federal power is perfect. The Power Rangers request is unexpected enough to land hard.

jokes.text: I'll run this up the flagpole. Also, can you bring back Power Rangers? I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough to get that done.
jokes.setup: Grant says he'll consider Leslie's proposal to work from Pawnee.
jokes.punchline: The Power Rangers request — addressed to a National Parks official as if he has general Important Person powers — is perfectly Andy energy.
jokes.explanation: Great Andy character joke. The assumption that federal importance is interchangeable — parks official = has Power Rangers authority — is perfectly Andy. 'I don't know what it is you do, but you seem important enough' is a great qualifier.

jokes.text: Sometimes you have to make the hardest climb to see the most beautiful sunrise. I read that once on an old lady's decorative pillow. But it is really how I feel today.
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving her talking-head summary of the episode's events.
jokes.punchline: The inspirational quote she leads with is attributed to a decorative pillow — but she fully endorses it anyway, collapsing the distinction between kitsch wisdom and genuine feeling.
jokes.explanation: A lovely Leslie joke that also functions as the episode's emotional coda. The source attribution (decorative pillow) is funny because it deflates the inspirational setup, but 'it is really how I feel today' re-earnests it. Very Leslie to find genuine meaning in literal sofa cushion philosophy.

jokes.text: Sometimes you have to make the hardest climb to see the most beautiful sunrise. I read that once on an old lady's decorative pillow.
jokes.setup: Leslie is delivering a talking-head confessional about her journey to the decision.
jokes.punchline: After delivering what sounds like a genuine inspirational sentiment, she sources it to 'an old lady's decorative pillow' — undercutting the profundity while simultaneously endorsing it.
jokes.explanation: Excellent Leslie talking-head joke. The source citation — 'an old lady's decorative pillow' — is a perfect subversion of inspirational-speech territory, and Leslie's 'but it is really how I feel today' reveals she genuinely means it, which makes the decorative pillow source even funnier. High economy, great character integration.

jokes.text: Ed, you're a nice guy, but you're the most incompetent person I've ever worked with. And that includes Terry. / Jeez. Get it together, Terry. / Clean out your desk. You're fired.
jokes.setup: In a time-jump flash-forward, Leslie is dealing with a new incompetent employee named Ed.
jokes.punchline: Leslie compares Ed's incompetence unfavorably to Terry/Larry — the office's longstanding punching bag — and when someone tells Terry to 'get it together,' the implication is that Terry agrees.
jokes.explanation: Good flash-forward Larry/Terry gag. The revelation that someone can be more incompetent than Larry is funny on its own, but 'Jeez. Get it together, Terry' from someone in the room who overhears the comparison is the better beat — Terry being used as a benchmark for failure, and apparently taking criticism for it.

jokes.text: Ben, how many bags of marshmallows do I give them? / None. Just let April do everything. / Oh, God, one day in the distant future, things will be calm and normal, right? / Probably not. But that's okay.
jokes.setup: Andy is babysitting Leslie and Ben's kids and needs guidance.
jokes.punchline: The implicit horror of Andy in charge of marshmallow quantities, Ben's solution (let April handle everything, which is its own problem), and Leslie's existential question answered with 'Probably not. But that's okay.'
jokes.explanation: Warm closing joke. The marshmallow question establishes Andy's childlike incompetence; Ben's solution (April) creates a new problem; Leslie's existential check-in is answered with perfect Parks & Rec optimism-in-chaos. 'Probably not. But that's okay.' is a lovely character beat for Ben.

jokes.text: Ben, how many bags of marshmallows do I give them? / None. Just let April do everything.
jokes.setup: Andy and April are babysitting Leslie and Ben's triplets while they handle a crisis.
jokes.punchline: 'None. Just let April do everything.' — Ben's complete delegation of parenting to April, combined with the implied insanity of what April might do, is the joke. Also 'how many bags of marshmallows' as a quantity implying multiple bags were on the table.
jokes.explanation: Good double joke. The marshmallow question implies Andy's instinct was to feed children industrial quantities of marshmallows, and Ben's 'just let April do everything' is simultaneously trusting and terrifying given April's character.

jokes.text: Oh, God, one day in the distant future, things will be calm and normal, right? / Probably not. But that's okay.
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are running to handle a new crisis amid their already chaotic lives.
jokes.punchline: Ben's 'probably not' — a calm, honest assessment that their lives will never be calm — delivered not as a complaint but as an acceptable fact.
jokes.explanation: Beautiful series-finale-appropriate joke. 'Probably not. But that's okay.' is a perfect closing character beat — Ben's calm acceptance of permanent chaos as the price of their life together. Works as both a joke and an emotional payoff.

insight: Season finale leans on character comfort over comedy peaks at 77.8.
